commercial_incentive: appears to be part of a structured course/lecture series; no explicit sales pitch within this clip itself
key_insights: Recommends applying to 6-8 schools, with 10 as an upper limit, arguing quality of application effort matters more than quantity of applications.
Defines a school as automatically a 'reach for everyone' if its acceptance rate is 25% or lower, regardless of the applicant's own stats.
Defines a personal reach as any school whose stated GPA/test requirements exceed the student's own qualifications (e.g., school wants 3.5 GPA, student has 3.0).
Defines target/match schools as those where the student's GPA/test scores closely match the school's stated requirements.

Defines safety schools as those where the student's qualifications exceed the school's requirements, and argues students should value safeties as much as reach schools rather than treating 'safety' as a negative label.
Suggests further subdividing reach/target/safety into 'high' and 'low' bands using acceptance-rate cutoffs (e.g., ~10% acceptance = high reach, ~25% = low/plain reach).

Advises every list include at least two safety schools so the student has guaranteed options regardless of reach/target outcomes, and suggests choosing safeties that share qualities (location, facilities) with liked reach schools.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Recommended application count: 6-8 schools, 10 maximum (stated by presenter)
Schools with acceptance rate ~25% or below are classified as automatic reach schools (stated by presenter)
A ~10% acceptance rate is characterized as 'high reach' versus ~25% as a lower-tier reach (stated by presenter)
notable_or_distinctive: Explicitly ties the reach/target/safety labels to concrete acceptance-rate percentage cutoffs and adds a 'high/low' subdivision system, which is more quantitatively specific than most generic reach/match/safety explainers.
reliability_notes: Generic lecture-style advice with filler analogies (water bottle, walking and chewing gum); acceptance-rate thresholds are presented as the instructor's own rule of thumb, not sourced from official data, and the video is 8 years old so selectivity at many schools has since increased.
